claim: Neurons of the mouse medial (fastigial) cerebellar nuclei (mCbN) fire spontaneously with wide dynamic ranges.
source: Here, we find that neurons of the mouse medial (fastigial) cerebellar nuclei (mCbN), which fire spontaneously with wide dynamic ranges, send glutamatergic projections to the ventrolateral periaqueductal gray (vlPAG), which contains diverse cell types.
evidence: Supported by electrophysiological recordings showing spontaneous firing rates and frequency-intensity curves of mCbN neurons.

claim: mCbN neurons send glutamatergic projections to the ventrolateral periaqueductal gray (vlPAG).
source: Here, we find that neurons of the mouse medial (fastigial) cerebellar nuclei (mCbN), which fire spontaneously with wide dynamic ranges, send glutamatergic projections to the ventrolateral periaqueductal gray (vlPAG), which contains diverse cell types.
evidence: Supported by viral tracing experiments showing axonal labeling in vlPAG after mCbN injection and optogenetically-evoked EPSCs.

claim: The vlPAG contains diverse cell types.
source: Here, we find that neurons of the mouse medial (fastigial) cerebellar nuclei (mCbN), which fire spontaneously with wide dynamic ranges, send glutamatergic projections to the ventrolateral periaqueductal gray (vlPAG), which contains diverse cell types.
evidence: Supported by recordings from multiple cell types (Chx10, GAD2, TH) in the vlPAG.

claim: Optogenetically stimulating glutamatergic vlPAG neurons that express Chx10 reliably induces freezing in freely moving mice.
source: In freely moving mice, optogenetically stimulating glutamatergic vlPAG neurons that express Chx10 reliably induces freezing.
evidence: Supported by behavioral experiments showing cessation of movement during optogenetic stimulation of Chx10 neurons.

claim: mCbN terminals excite approximately 20% of neurons positive for Chx10 in vlPAG slices.
source: In vlPAG slices, mCbN terminals excite ~20% of neurons positive for Chx10 or GAD2 and ~70% of dopaminergic TH-positive neurons.
evidence: Supported by electrophysiological recordings showing EPSCs in 20% of Chx10 neurons upon optogenetic stimulation of mCbN terminals.

claim: mCbN terminals excite approximately 20% of neurons positive for GAD2 in vlPAG slices.
source: In vlPAG slices, mCbN terminals excite ~20% of neurons positive for Chx10 or GAD2 and ~70% of dopaminergic TH-positive neurons.
evidence: Supported by electrophysiological recordings showing EPSCs in 21% of GAD2 neurons upon optogenetic stimulation of mCbN terminals.

claim: mCbN terminals excite approximately 70% of dopaminergic TH-positive neurons in vlPAG slices.
source: In vlPAG slices, mCbN terminals excite ~20% of neurons positive for Chx10 or GAD2 and ~70% of dopaminergic TH-positive neurons.
evidence: Supported by electrophysiological recordings showing EPSCs in 72.7% of TH neurons upon optogenetic stimulation of mCbN terminals.

claim: Stimulating mCbN afferents augments IPSCs in Chx10 neurons by activating postsynaptic D2 receptors.
source: Stimulating either mCbN afferents or TH neurons augments IPSCs and suppresses EPSCs in Chx10 neurons by activating postsynaptic D2 receptors.
evidence: Supported by electrophysiological recordings showing increased IPSCs during mCbN stimulation, mimicked by D2 agonist and blocked by D2 antagonist.

claim: Stimulating mCbN afferents suppresses EPSCs in Chx10 neurons by activating postsynaptic D2 receptors.
source: Stimulating either mCbN afferents or TH neurons augments IPSCs and suppresses EPSCs in Chx10 neurons by activating postsynaptic D2 receptors.
evidence: Supported by electrophysiological recordings showing decreased EPSCs during mCbN stimulation, mimicked by D2 agonist and blocked by D2 antagonist.

claim: Stimulating TH neurons augments IPSCs in Chx10 neurons by activating postsynaptic D2 receptors.
source: Stimulating either mCbN afferents or TH neurons augments IPSCs and suppresses EPSCs in Chx10 neurons by activating postsynaptic D2 receptors.
evidence: Supported by electrophysiological recordings showing increased IPSCs during TH neuron stimulation, mimicked by D2 agonist and blocked by D2 antagonist.

claim: Stimulating TH neurons suppresses EPSCs in Chx10 neurons by activating postsynaptic D2 receptors.
source: Stimulating either mCbN afferents or TH neurons augments IPSCs and suppresses EPSCs in Chx10 neurons by activating postsynaptic D2 receptors.
evidence: Supported by electrophysiological recordings showing decreased EPSCs during TH neuron stimulation, mimicked by D2 agonist and blocked by D2 antagonist.

claim: mCbN activity regulates dopaminergic modulation of the vlPAG, favoring inhibition of Chx10 neurons.
source: The results suggest that mCbN activity regulates dopaminergic modulation of the vlPAG, favoring inhibition of Chx10 neurons.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that mCbN stimulation activates TH neurons, which in turn modulate PSCs in Chx10 neurons via D2 receptors to favor inhibition.

claim: Suppression of cerebellar output may facilitate freezing.
source: Suppression of cerebellar output may therefore facilitate freezing.
evidence: Speculated based on the finding that mCbN activity favors inhibition of Chx10 neurons, which drive freezing.

claim: Freezing is an adaptive behavior for avoiding predation.
source: Innate defensive behaviors, such as freezing, are adaptive for avoiding predation.
evidence: Based on established scientific knowledge about defensive behaviors.

claim: Freezing-related midbrain regions project to the cerebellum.
source: Freezing-related midbrain regions project to the cerebellum, which is known to regulate rapid sensorimotor integration, raising the question of cerebellar contributions to freezing.
evidence: Supported by citations to previous anatomical studies.

claim: The cerebellum is known to regulate rapid sensorimotor integration.
source: Freezing-related midbrain regions project to the cerebellum, which is known to regulate rapid sensorimotor integration, raising the question of cerebellar contributions to freezing.
evidence: Based on established scientific knowledge about cerebellar function.

claim: Animals must rapidly recognize and respond to threats to avoid predation.
source: To avoid predation, animals must rapidly recognize and respond to threats.
evidence: Based on established scientific knowledge about defensive behaviors.

claim: Defensive behaviors rely on innate neural circuitry to identify threatening stimuli within the context of the local environment.
source: Such defensive behaviors rely on innate neural circuitry both to identify the threatening stimulus within the context of the local environment and to engage one of multiple defensive behaviors, such as freezing or fleeing (Blanchard and Blanchard, 1972; De Franceschi et al., 2016; Fendt and Fanselow, 1999; LeDoux, 2000; Yilmaz and Meister, 2013), depending on the imminence of the threat (Perusini and Fanselow, 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies on defensive behaviors.

claim: Defensive behaviors rely on innate neural circuitry to engage one of multiple defensive behaviors, such as freezing or fleeing, depending on the imminence of the threat.
source: Such defensive behaviors rely on innate neural circuitry both to identify the threatening stimulus within the context of the local environment and to engage one of multiple defensive behaviors, such as freezing or fleeing (Blanchard and Blanchard, 1972; De Franceschi et al., 2016; Fendt and Fanselow, 1999; LeDoux, 2000; Yilmaz and Meister, 2013), depending on the imminence of the threat (Perusini and Fanselow, 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies on defensive behaviors.

claim: The specific defensive strategy that is selected is determined by which one of multiple rostro-caudal columns is activated within the periaqueductal gray.
source: At a neuronal level, the specific defensive strategy that is selected is determined by which one of multiple rostro-caudal columns is activated within the periaqueductal gray (Bandler et al., 2000; Bandler and Shipley, 1994; Carrive, 1993; Keay and Bandler, 2001; Koutsikou et al., 2017; Watson et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies on PAG organization.

claim: Freezing depends on the ventrolateral column of the periaqueductal gray (vlPAG).
source: Freezing, for example, depends on the ventrolateral column of the periaqueductal gray (vlPAG), which contains glutamatergic neurons whose activation elicits freezing and whose inactivation blocks non-associative, 'innate' freezing to intrinsically threatening stimuli (Tovote et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Tovote et al., 2016.

claim: The vlPAG contains glutamatergic neurons whose activation elicits freezing.
source: Freezing, for example, depends on the ventrolateral column of the periaqueductal gray (vlPAG), which contains glutamatergic neurons whose activation elicits freezing and whose inactivation blocks non-associative, 'innate' freezing to intrinsically threatening stimuli (Tovote et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Tovote et al., 2016.

claim: Inactivation of glutamatergic neurons in the vlPAG blocks non-associative, 'innate' freezing to intrinsically threatening stimuli.
source: Freezing, for example, depends on the ventrolateral column of the periaqueductal gray (vlPAG), which contains glutamatergic neurons whose activation elicits freezing and whose inactivation blocks non-associative, 'innate' freezing to intrinsically threatening stimuli (Tovote et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Tovote et al., 2016.

claim: vlPAG neurons participate in eliciting fear-related outputs.
source: In addition to eliciting fear-related outputs (Oka et al., 2008; Perusini and Fanselow, 2015; Tovote et al., 2015), recent evidence suggests that vlPAG neurons also participate in assessing threat probability (Wright and McDannald, 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: vlPAG neurons participate in assessing threat probability.
source: In addition to eliciting fear-related outputs (Oka et al., 2008; Perusini and Fanselow, 2015; Tovote et al., 2015), recent evidence suggests that vlPAG neurons also participate in assessing threat probability (Wright and McDannald, 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to Wright and McDannald, 2019.

claim: The vlPAG receives input from many brain areas, several of which participate in conditioned freezing, including the amygdala, hypothalamus, zona incerta and prefrontal cortex.
source: Consistent with its role in integrating complex, contextual sensory stimuli, the vlPAG receives input from many brain areas, several of which participate in conditioned freezing, including the amygdala, hypothalamus, zona incerta and prefrontal cortex (Tovote et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Tovote et al., 2015.

claim: The medial cerebellar nucleus (mCbN in rodents; the fastigial nucleus in primates) receives input from the cerebellar vermis.
source: Anatomically, the medial cerebellar nucleus (mCbN in rodents; the fastigial nucleus in primates), which receives input from the cerebellar vermis, projects to the vlPAG (Teune et al., 2000; Gonzalo-Ruiz et al., 1990).
evidence: Based on established anatomical knowledge.

claim: The medial cerebellar nucleus projects to the vlPAG.
source: Anatomically, the medial cerebellar nucleus (mCbN in rodents; the fastigial nucleus in primates), which receives input from the cerebellar vermis, projects to the vlPAG (Teune et al., 2000; Gonzalo-Ruiz et al., 1990).
evidence: Supported by citations to Teune et al., 2000 and Gonzalo-Ruiz et al., 1990.

claim: The mCbN projection to the vlPAG has been attributed primarily to oculomotor function.
source: Although this projection has been attributed primarily to oculomotor function, lesions of the cerebellar vermis lead to decreases in both innate and conditioned freezing in rodents (Supple et al., 1988; Koutsikou et al., 2014; Sacchetti et al., 2002).
evidence: Based on previous interpretations in the literature.

claim: Lesions of the cerebellar vermis lead to decreases in both innate and conditioned freezing in rodents.
source: Although this projection has been attributed primarily to oculomotor function, lesions of the cerebellar vermis lead to decreases in both innate and conditioned freezing in rodents (Supple et al., 1988; Koutsikou et al., 2014; Sacchetti et al., 2002).
evidence: Supported by citations to Supple et al., 1988; Koutsikou et al., 2014; Sacchetti et al., 2002.

claim: The cerebellum participates in perception of potential threats, prediction of threat probability, and/or execution of innate or conditioned freezing behavior.
source: Given known roles of the cerebellum in sensorimotor integration, it seems plausible that it may participate in perception of potential threats, prediction of threat probability, and/or execution of innate or conditioned freezing behavior.
evidence: Speculated based on known cerebellar functions and anatomical connections.

claim: Fear conditioning leads to potentiation of parallel fiber synapses onto vermal Purkinje cells.
source: Indeed, consistent with the well-established role of the cerebellum in associative learning, fear conditioning leads to potentiation of parallel fiber synapses onto vermal Purkinje cells, and deficits in cerebellar plasticity disrupt fear recall (Sacchetti et al., 2004).
evidence: Supported by citation to Sacchetti et al., 2004.

claim: Deficits in cerebellar plasticity disrupt fear recall.
source: Indeed, consistent with the well-established role of the cerebellum in associative learning, fear conditioning leads to potentiation of parallel fiber synapses onto vermal Purkinje cells, and deficits in cerebellar plasticity disrupt fear recall (Sacchetti et al., 2004).
evidence: Supported by citation to Sacchetti et al., 2004.

claim: The cerebellum regulates movement.
source: More generally, the cerebellum regulates movement, and freezing is a motor behavior characterized by the suppression of voluntary motion (Koutsikou et al., 2014), raising the possibility of a more fundamental cerebellar role in innate freezing.
evidence: Based on established scientific knowledge about cerebellar function.

claim: Freezing is a motor behavior characterized by the suppression of voluntary motion.
source: More generally, the cerebellum regulates movement, and freezing is a motor behavior characterized by the suppression of voluntary motion (Koutsikou et al., 2014), raising the possibility of a more fundamental cerebellar role in innate freezing.
evidence: Supported by citation to Koutsikou et al., 2014.

claim: Injecting the mCbN with viruses expressing ChR2-eYFP results in axonal labeling in the caudal-most aspect of the vlPAG.
source: First, we injected the mCbN with viruses expressing a channelrhodopsin-eYFP (ChR2-eYFP) fusion protein (Figure 1A, left, middle). After 4–6 weeks, axonal labeling was evident in the caudal-most aspect of the vlPAG, consistent with a direct projection (Figure 1A, right).
evidence: Supported by anatomical tracing data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Axonal labeling from mCbN has the highest density in the caudal ~600–900 μm of the vlPAG, ventral and lateral to the central aqueduct.
source: Axonal labeling had the highest density in the caudal ~600–900 μm of the vlPAG, ventral and lateral to the central aqueduct, with sparser axonal labeling near the aqueduct (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by anatomical data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Injecting the vlPAG with CTb-GFP or retrobeads results in retrograde labeling of large neurons in the mCbN.
source: Conversely, injecting the vlPAG with either CTb-GFP or retrobeads (Figure 1B, left, middle) resulted in retrograde labeling of large neurons in the mCbN (Figure 1B, right).
evidence: Supported by anatomical tracing data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Following a unilateral injection of retrograde tracer in the vlPAG, the greatest labeling density is in the contralateral mCbN, although some ipsilateral labeling is also evident.
source: Following a unilateral injection of retrograde tracer, the greatest labeling density was in the contralateral mCbN, although some ipsilateral labeling was also evident.
evidence: Supported by anatomical tracing data.

claim: Retrogradely labeled neurons were not observed in the neighboring interpositus or lateral cerebellar nucleus after vlPAG injection.
source: Retrogradely labeled neurons were not observed in the neighboring interpositus or lateral cerebellar nucleus, suggesting specificity of the projection from the mCbN to the vlPAG.
evidence: Supported by anatomical tracing data.

claim: Chx10 neurons are enriched in the vlPAG.
source: Chx10 neurons were enriched in the vlPAG (Figure 1C), and injecting viruses with cre-dependent transgene expression into the vlPAG of Chx10-cre mice (Figure 1D) resulted in relatively selective axonal labeling in the Mc (Figure 1E), with few labeled fibers in the more dorsal nucleus gigantocellularis.
evidence: Supported by anatomical data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Injecting viruses with cre-dependent transgene expression into the vlPAG of Chx10-cre mice results in relatively selective axonal labeling in the magnocellular reticular nucleus (Mc).
source: Chx10 neurons were enriched in the vlPAG (Figure 1C), and injecting viruses with cre-dependent transgene expression into the vlPAG of Chx10-cre mice (Figure 1D) resulted in relatively selective axonal labeling in the Mc (Figure 1E), with few labeled fibers in the more dorsal nucleus gigantocellularis.
evidence: Supported by anatomical data shown in Figure 1D and 1E.

claim: Chx10 labeled axons have the highest density at the rostral-caudal level of the inferior olive.
source: Chx10 labeled axons, however, were primarily caudal to the traditional RVM circuitry, having the highest density at the rostal-caudal level of the inferior olive, making it seem unlikely that these cells participate in the anti-nociceptive pathway from the vlPAG.
evidence: Supported by anatomical tracing data.

claim: Light stimulation of Chx10 neurons results in inward currents in Mc neurons.
source: Light stimulation of Chx10 neurons resulted in inward currents of −68.7 ± 9.6 pA at −70 mV in Mc neurons, consistent with glutamatergic synapses (Figure 1F; n = 7 cells [5 M, 2 F]).
evidence: Supported by electrophysiological recordings shown in Figure 1F.

claim: The paired pulse ratio of Chx10-evoked responses in Mc neurons is 0.7 ± 0.4.
source: In the 4 cells in which pairs of responses were evoked (40 ms interval), the paired pulse ratio was 0.7 ± 0.4.
evidence: Supported by electrophysiological recordings.

claim: 50 Hz trains of 100 light stimuli elicit photocurrents that are relatively stable in Chx10 neurons under voltage clamp.
source: Indeed, in Chx10 neurons (n = 9 cells, [9M, 0F]), 50 Hz trains of 100 light stimuli (10 ms pulses) elicited photocurrents that were relatively stable under voltage clamp (1st current, −78.5 ± 8.6 pA; 5th and 100th current, 73.1 ± 2.0% and 66.0 ± 1.7% of 1st current).
evidence: Supported by electrophysiological recordings in slices.

claim: 50 Hz light stimulation brings Chx10 neuron firing rates from 3.8 ± 3.9 spikes/sec to 20.5 ± 3.6 spikes/sec under current-clamp.
source: Under current-clamp, the same stimulation brought firing rates from 3.8 ± 3.9 spikes/sec to 20.5 ± 3.6 spikes/sec, with elevated spike rates persisting throughout stimulation (Figure 2A,B).
evidence: Supported by electrophysiological recordings shown in Figure 2A and 2B.

claim: Light trains applied for 2–5 s result in a nearly complete cessation of movement in Chx10-ChR2 mice.
source: Light trains as in slices (10 ms pulses at 50 Hz) applied for 2–5 s resulted in a nearly complete cessation of movement in Chx10-ChR2 mice, which persisted for the duration of optogenetic stimulation (n = 7 mice, 50 trials per mouse; Figure 2E, left).
evidence: Supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Visual inspection of the behavior during optogenetic stimulation of Chx10 neurons was consistent with freezing, as mice ceased all voluntary movements with the exception of respiration, eye movements, and some whisking.
source: Visual inspection of the behavior was consistent with freezing, as mice ceased all voluntary movements with the exception of respiration, eye movements, and some whisking (Video 1).
evidence: Supported by video evidence (Video 1).

claim: Freezing was elicited regardless of the ongoing motor behavior of the mouse.
source: Freezing was elicited regardless of the ongoing motor behavior of the mouse, and was rarely accompanied by threat assessment behavior or continued freezing after stimulus termination, consistent with the idea that Chx10 vlPAG activation was not aversive but directly evoked a motor program.
evidence: Supported by behavioral observations.

claim: Chx10 vlPAG activation directly evokes a motor program rather than being aversive.
source: Freezing was elicited regardless of the ongoing motor behavior of the mouse, and was rarely accompanied by threat assessment behavior or continued freezing after stimulus termination, consistent with the idea that Chx10 vlPAG activation was not aversive but directly evoked a motor program.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that freezing was not accompanied by threat assessment behavior or continued after stimulus termination.

claim: In control mice, optogenetic stimuli have no detectable effect on ongoing movement.
source: Conversely, in control mice (n = 7 mice), optogenetic stimuli had no detectable effect on ongoing movement (Figure 2E, right).
evidence: Supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Movement falls by >3 standard deviations in Chx10-ChR2 mice during optogenetic stimulation but is unchanged in control mice.
source: Relative to the mean baseline movement for 2 s before optogenetic stimulation, movement fell by >3 standard deviations (SDs) in Chx10-ChR2 mice but was unchanged in control mice (Figure 2F).
evidence: Supported by quantitative behavioral data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: The latency to a 3-SD drop in movement during optogenetic stimulation of Chx10 neurons is 660 ± 30 ms.
source: We therefore measured the latency to a 3-SD drop, which was 660 ± 30 ms (~2.5 frames).
evidence: Supported by quantitative behavioral data.

claim: In the pre-stimulus baseline, immobility is comparable in Chx10-ChR2 and control mice (35.9 ± 6.2% and 37.4 ± 4.2%, respectively).
source: In the pre-stimulus baseline, immobility was comparable in Chx10-ChR2 and control mice (35.9 ± 6.2% and 37.4 ± 4.2%, respectively, n = 7 mice per group).
evidence: Supported by quantitative behavioral data.

claim: During stimulation, immobility increases to 92.8 ± 2.5% in Chx10-ChR2 mice but remains at 37.6 ± 3.9% in control mice.
source: During stimulation, immobility increased to 92.8 ± 2.5% in Chx10-ChR2 mice (p=<0.001, paired t-test) but remained at 37.6 ± 3.9% in control mice (p=0.84, paired t-test; Chx10-ChR2 vs. control, p=<0.0001, unpaired t-test, Figure 2G).
evidence: Supported by quantitative behavioral data shown in Figure 2G.

claim: The duration of immobility and of light stimulation are strongly correlated (r2 = 0.98) with a slope near unity (0.9).
source: The duration of immobility and of light stimulation were strongly correlated (Figure 2H, r2 = 0.98), with a slope near unity (0.9) suggesting that freezing and Chx10 neuronal firing are directly related.
evidence: Supported by quantitative behavioral data shown in Figure 2H.

claim: Repeated optogenetic stimulation (50 trials, 20 s inter-trial interval) of Chx10 neurons reliably elicits freezing without habituation.
source: Finally, consistent with a role in directly evoking the freezing motor pattern, repeated optogenetic stimulation (50 trials, 20 s inter-trial interval) of Chx10 neurons reliably elicited freezing, without habituation (Figure 2I; stimuli 1–5: 92.2 ± 2.2%; stimuli 46–50: 92.0 ± 1.3%, p=0.9, unpaired t-test).
evidence: Supported by quantitative behavioral data shown in Figure 2I.

claim: Chx10 neurons have input resistances of 584.1 ± 47.3 MΩ.
source: Chx10 neurons were electrically tight, with input resistances of 584.1 ± 47.3 MΩ and capacitances of 24.2 ± 1.3 pF (n = 26 cells [15 M, 11 F]).
evidence: Supported by electrophysiological recordings.

claim: Chx10 neurons have capacitances of 24.2 ± 1.3 pF.
source: Chx10 neurons were electrically tight, with input resistances of 584.1 ± 47.3 MΩ and capacitances of 24.2 ± 1.3 pF (n = 26 cells [15 M, 11 F]).
evidence: Supported by electrophysiological recordings.

claim: Current-clamped Chx10 neurons fire spontaneously at 5.8 ± 1.2 spikes/s.
source: Current-clamped Chx10 neurons fired spontaneously at 5.8 ± 1.2 spikes/s (Figure 3A,B; n = 28 cells).
evidence: Supported by electrophysiological recordings shown in Figure 3A and 3B.

claim: GAD2+ neurons recorded in the vlPAG fire more rapidly than Chx10 neurons, at 20.7 ± 3.2 spikes/sec.
source: In contrast GAD2+ neurons recorded in the vlPAG fired more rapidly, at 20.7 ± 3.2 spikes/sec (Figure 3—figure supplement 1; n = 16 cells [8 M, 8 F], Chx10 vs. GAD2, p=0.0003; unpaired t-test).
evidence: Supported by electrophysiological recordings shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: In Chx10 neurons, spikes are broad (half-width: 1.0 ± 0.05 ms) and lack afterhyperpolarizations.
source: In Chx10 neurons, spikes were broad (half-width: 1.0 ± 0.05 ms, n = 26 cells [15 M, 11 F]) and lacked afterhyperpolarizations, whereas those of GAD2+ vlPAG neurons were briefer, with prominent afterhyperpolarizations (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by electrophysiological recordings shown in Figure 3C, 3D, and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: GAD2+ vlPAG neurons have briefer spikes with prominent afterhyperpolarizations compared to Chx10 neurons.
source: In Chx10 neurons, spikes were broad (half-width: 1.0 ± 0.05 ms, n = 26 cells [15 M, 11 F]) and lacked afterhyperpolarizations, whereas those of GAD2+ vlPAG neurons were briefer, with prominent afterhyperpolarizations (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by electrophysiological recordings shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Chx10 neurons can be silenced with a few tens of pA of hyperpolarizing current.
source: Hyperpolarizing and depolarizing current injections (−100 to 100 pA, 10 pA steps) illustrated that Chx10 neurons could be silenced with a few tens of pA and their firing rate began to saturate above 60 pA (Figure 3E,F; max rate with 100 pA: 48 ± 3.6 spikes/sec, n = 26 cells).
evidence: Supported by electrophysiological recordings shown in Figure 3E and 3F.

claim: The maximum firing rate of Chx10 neurons with 100 pA injected current is 48 ± 3.6 spikes/sec.
source: Hyperpolarizing and depolarizing current injections (−100 to 100 pA, 10 pA steps) illustrated that Chx10 neurons could be silenced with a few tens of pA and their firing rate began to saturate above 60 pA (Figure 3E,F; max rate with 100 pA: 48 ± 3.6 spikes/sec, n = 26 cells).
evidence: Supported by electrophysiological recordings shown in Figure 3E and 3F.

claim: The slope of the FI curve between 0 and 50 pA of injected current in Chx10 neurons is 7.6 ± 0.8 spikes/pA.
source: The relatively steep slope of the FI curve between 0 and 50 pA of injected current (7.6 ± 0.8 spikes/pA) suggests that even small synaptic inputs may be sufficient to drive action potential firing in Chx10 cells.
evidence: Supported by electrophysiological recordings.

claim: eEPSCs at −70 mV in Chx10 neurons have an amplitude of −250.8 ± 100.1 pA.
source: eEPSCs at −70 mV had an amplitude of −250.8 ± 7 00.1 pA and eIPSCs at 0 mV had an amplitude of 322.2 ± 90.3 pA (Figure 3G; n = 12 cells [12 M, 0 F]).
evidence: Supported by electrophysiological recordings shown in Figure 3G.

claim: eIPSCs at 0 mV in Chx10 neurons have an amplitude of 322.2 ± 90.3 pA.
source: eEPSCs at −70 mV had an amplitude of −250.8 ± 7 00.1 pA and eIPSCs at 0 mV had an amplitude of 322.2 ± 90.3 pA (Figure 3G; n = 12 cells [12 M, 0 F]).
evidence: Supported by electrophysiological recordings shown in Figure 3G.

claim: The peak excitatory conductance in Chx10 neurons is 17.6 ± 4.9 nS and the peak inhibitory conductance is 22.6 ± 6.3 nS.
source: Comparing the peak excitatory and inhibitory conductances in each cell indicated that the strength of inhibition and excitation were comparable, with a slight bias toward inhibition (Figure 3H; E vs. I: 17.6 ± 4.9 nS vs. 22.6 ± 6.3 nS, p=0.08, paired t-test), giving an E/I ratio of 0.78.
evidence: Supported by electrophysiological recordings shown in Figure 3H.

claim: The E/I ratio in Chx10 neurons is 0.78.
source: Comparing the peak excitatory and inhibitory conductances in each cell indicated that the strength of inhibition and excitation were comparable, with a slight bias toward inhibition (Figure 3H; E vs. I: 17.6 ± 4.9 nS vs. 22.6 ± 6.3 nS, p=0.08, paired t-test), giving an E/I ratio of 0.78.
evidence: Calculated from the ratio of excitatory to inhibitory conductances.

claim: eEPSCs in Chx10 neurons decay with a single exponential time constant, τ, of 3.5 ± 0.3 ms.
source: eEPSCs decayed with a single exponential time constant, τ, of 3.5 ± 0.3 ms (Figure 3I) whereas eIPSCs were nearly twice as long (6.7 ± 0.6 ms; Figure 3I).
evidence: Supported by electrophysiological recordings shown in Figure 3I.

claim: eIPSCs in Chx10 neurons decay with a time constant of 6.7 ± 0.6 ms.
source: eEPSCs decayed with a single exponential time constant, τ, of 3.5 ± 0.3 ms (Figure 3I) whereas eIPSCs were nearly twice as long (6.7 ± 0.6 ms; Figure 3I).
evidence: Supported by electrophysiological recordings shown in Figure 3I.

claim: mCbN neurons fire spontaneously at high rates (122.8 ± 6.6 spikes/s).
source: As in the interpositus nucleus (iCbN; Mercer et al., 2016; Person and Raman, 2012; Raman et al., 2000), mCbN neurons fired spontaneously at high rates (Figure 4A; 122.8 ± 6.6 spikes/s, n = 28 cells [15 M, 13 F]), consistent with previous reports of mCbN projection neurons in vitro (Bagnall et al., 2009) as well as the high basal activity of mCbN cells in vivo (Büttner et al., 1991; Miller et al., 2008; Özcan et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by electrophysiological recordings shown in Figure 4A and citations to previous studies.

claim: Spontaneous firing rates of mCbN neurons are higher in males (137.4 ± 8.8 spikes/s) than females (105.9 ± 9.0 spikes/s).
source: Interestingly, spontaneous rates were higher in males (137.4 ± 8.8 spikes/s, n = 15 cells) than females (105.9 ± 9.0 spikes/s, n = 13 cells, p=0.01, unpaired t-test, Figure 4A,B), a difference that is in the opposite direction from the sex difference in the iCbN (Mercer et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by electrophysiological recordings shown in Figure 4A and 4B.

claim: The sex difference in mCbN firing rates is in the opposite direction from the sex difference in the iCbN.
source: Interestingly, spontaneous rates were higher in males (137.4 ± 8.8 spikes/s, n = 15 cells) than females (105.9 ± 9.0 spikes/s, n = 13 cells, p=0.01, unpaired t-test, Figure 4A,B), a difference that is in the opposite direction from the sex difference in the iCbN (Mercer et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by comparison with data from Mercer et al., 2016.

claim: Comparing the firing rates between mCbN and iCbN shows a nearly twofold difference in males (iCbN: 72.2 ± 10.0 spikes/s vs. mCbN: 137.4 ± 8.8 spikes/s) but no difference for females (iCbN: 97.7 ± 9.2 spikes/s vs. mCbN: 105.9 ± 9.0 spikes/s).
source: In fact, comparing the firing rates between the two nuclei showed a nearly twofold difference in males (iCbN: 72.2 ± 10.0 spikes/s, n = 15 cells, p=0.00004, unpaired t-test) but no difference for females (iCbN: 97.7 ± 9.2 spikes/s, n = 16 cells, p=0.51, unpaired t-test; iCbN data from Mercer et al., 2016, Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by comparison with data from Mercer et al., 2016, shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Spontaneous action potentials in mCbN neurons have a half-width of 0.26 ± 0.02 ms.
source: Half-width analysis indicated that spontaneous action potentials were brief (Figure 4C; 0.26 ± 0.02 ms) and phase-plane plots estimated a threshold of −42.3 ± 0.7 mV (Figure 4D).
evidence: Supported by electrophysiological recordings shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Phase-plane plots estimate a threshold of −42.3 ± 0.7 mV for mCbN neurons.
source: Half-width analysis indicated that spontaneous action potentials were brief (Figure 4C; 0.26 ± 0.02 ms) and phase-plane plots estimated a threshold of −42.3 ± 0.7 mV (Figure 4D).
evidence: Supported by electrophysiological recordings shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Firing rates of mCbN neurons change linearly with current injections from −300 to +300 pA, with a slope of 0.36 ± 0.005 spikes/pA.
source: Firing rates changed linearly with current injections from −300 to +300 pA (500 ms steps), with a slope of 0.36 ± 0.005 spikes/pA (Figure 4E,F; n = 22 cells [12 M, 10 F]).
evidence: Supported by electrophysiological recordings shown in Figure 4E and 4F.

claim: The maximum firing rate of mCbN neurons with a peak injection of +300 pA is 227.9 ± 10.9 spikes/s.
source: The maximum firing rate with a peak injection of +300 pA was 227.9 ± 10.9 spikes/s (n = 22 cells), with little evidence of saturation, suggesting that mCbN neuron firing rates can be elevated as well as suppressed over a wide dynamic range.
evidence: Supported by electrophysiological recordings.

claim: IPSCs evoked in mCbN neurons by stimulating Purkinje cells have an amplitude of 3.0 ± 2.7 nA at 0 mV, reflecting a maximal conductance of 42.5 ± 10.2 nS.
source: In fact, large IPSCs were evoked in mCbN neurons by stimulating Purkinje cells either electrically (n = 7 cells [3 M, 4 F]) or with light in L7-ChR2 mice (n = 7 cells [0 M, 7 F]); since both procedures elicited comparable responses, the data were pooled, (Figure 4G,H). IPSCs at 0 mV were 3.0 ± 2.7 nA, reflecting a maximal conductance of 42.5 ± 10.2 nS, and had a τ of 4.2 ± 0.3 ms (Figure 4I), a value that is significantly longer than in the iCbN (Figure 4—figure supplement 1; iCbN: 2.14 ± 0.1 ms, n = 34 cells [22 M, 12 F], p<0.00001, unpaired t-test; iCbN data from Mercer et al. (2016).
evidence: Supported by electrophysiological recordings shown in Figure 4G and 4H.

claim: IPSCs in mCbN neurons have a τ of 4.2 ± 0.3 ms, which is significantly longer than in the iCbN (2.14 ± 0.1 ms).
source: IPSCs at 0 mV were 3.0 ± 2.7 nA, reflecting a maximal conductance of 42.5 ± 10.2 nS, and had a τ of 4.2 ± 0.3 ms (Figure 4I), a value that is significantly longer than in the iCbN (Figure 4—figure supplement 1; iCbN: 2.14 ± 0.1 ms, n = 34 cells [22 M, 12 F], p<0.00001, unpaired t-test; iCbN data from Mercer et al. (2016).
evidence: Supported by electrophysiological recordings shown in Figure 4I and Figure 4—figure supplement 1, and comparison with data from Mercer et al., 2016.

claim: The relatively slower kinetics of IPSCs in mCbN may make mCbN cells more readily suppressed by afferent Purkinje cells.
source: The relatively slower kinetics may make mCbN cells more readily suppressed by afferent Purkinje cells, since the efficacy of inhibition is highly dependent on IPSC time course (Person and Raman, 2012; Najac and Raman, 2015; Wu and Raman, 2017; Brown and Raman, 2018).
evidence: Inferred from the observation of slower IPSC kinetics and citations to previous studies on the relationship between IPSC time course and inhibition efficacy.

claim: Light stimulation of ChR2-labeled mCbN axons in the vlPAG elicits EPSCs at −70 mV in 11% of unidentified cells, 20% of Chx10 cells, and 21% of GAD2+ cells.
source: Light stimulation of ChR2-labeled mCbN axons in the vlPAG elicited EPSCs at −70 mV in only a subset of unidentified (11%, n = 4 of 38 cells), Chx10 (20%, n = 5 of 25 cells), and GAD2+ (21%, n = 3 of 14 cells) cells.
evidence: Supported by electrophysiological recordings.

claim: In cells in which an EPSC was evoked by mCbN stimulation, the direct mCbN-evoked synaptic currents have similar amplitudes across unidentified, Chx10, and GAD2+ cells.
source: In cells in which an EPSC was evoked, the direct mCbN-evoked synaptic currents had similar amplitudes across all three categories (Figure 5A,B; unidentified: −40.6 ± 15.4 pA, n = 4 cells; Chx10: −33.9 ± 9.7 pA, n = 5 cells; GAD2+: 39.6 ± 16.7 pA, n = 3 cells).
evidence: Supported by electrophysiological recordings shown in Figure 5A and 5B.

claim: mCbN stimulation never evokes detectable IPSCs in vlPAG cells.
source: Regardless of whether or not the cell received a direct EPSC, mCbN stimulation never evoked detectable IPSCs (n = 42 of 42 cells).
evidence: Supported by electrophysiological recordings.

claim: The projection from mCbN to the vlPAG is glutamatergic.
source: Thus, although some mCbN projection neurons are glycinergic (Bagnall et al., 2009), the projection to the vlPAG is glutamatergic.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that mCbN stimulation evokes EPSCs but not IPSCs in vlPAG cells.

claim: mCbN optogenetic stimulation increases the amplitude of eIPSCs in Chx10 neurons from 233.1 ± 49.9 pA to 280.7 ± 53.4 pA, corresponding to a within-cell increase of 28.7 ± 7.0%.
source: Indeed, mCbN optogenetic stimulation increased the amplitude of eIPSCs in Chx10 neurons from 233.1 ± 49.9 pA to 280.7 ± 53.4 pA (Figure 5C, n = 12 cells [10 M, 2 F]), corresponding to a within-cell increase of 28.7 ± 07.0% (Figure 5D, left; p=0.0016, one-sample t-test).
evidence: Supported by electrophysiological recordings shown in Figure 5C and 5D.

claim: The increased IPSC amplitude during mCbN stimulation occurs without a corresponding change in the paired-pulse ratio.
source: The increased IPSC amplitude occurred without a corresponding change in the paired-pulse ratio (PPR), which went from 1.03 ± 0.08 to 1.02 ± 0.07 (Figure 5D, right, n = 12 cells; p=0.94, paired t-test).
evidence: Supported by electrophysiological recordings shown in Figure 5D.

claim: mCbN stimulation decreases eEPSCs in Chx10 cells from −401.4 ± 55.2 pA to −355.6 ± 55.3 pA, a reduction of 13.7 ± 4.3%.
source: Additionally, mCbN stimulation had the converse effect on eEPSCs in Chx10 cells, decreasing them from −401.4 ± 55.2 pA to −355.6 ± 55.3 pA (Figure 5E, n = 12 cells [3 M, 9 F]), a reduction of 13.7 ± 4.3% (Figure 5F, left; p=0.0075, one sample t-test), again without a change in PPR (Figure 5F, right; 0.83 ± 0.07 to 0.88 ± 0.07; p=0.15, paired t-test).
evidence: Supported by electrophysiological recordings shown in Figure 5E and 5F.

claim: Modulation of PSC amplitude by mCbN stimulation is reliable, leading to a change of >10% in the majority of Chx10 cells (11/12 for IPSCs and 9/12 for EPSCs).
source: Modulation of PSC amplitude by mCbN stimulation was reliable, leading to a change of >10% in the majority of Chx10 cells (11/12 for IPSCs and 9/12 for EPSCs).
evidence: Supported by electrophysiological recordings.

claim: Before mCbN stimulation, the within-cell EI ratio in Chx10 cells is 0.78; after stimulation, the EI ratio is predicted to fall to 0.53, a 32.5% decrease.
source: Before stimulation, the within-cell EI ratio in Chx10 cells was 0.78 (17.6/22.6 nS); the mean percent change in excitation and inhibition predicts that, after stimulation, the EI ratio would fall to 0.53, i.e., a 32.5% decrease.
evidence: Calculated from the observed changes in excitatory and inhibitory conductances.

claim: The vlPAG includes a mixed population of dopaminergic and noradrenergic tyrosine hydroxylase (TH) positive neurons.
source: The vlPAG includes a mixed population of dopaminergic and noradrenergic tyrosine hydroxylase (TH) positive neurons (Figure 6A; Suckow et al., 2013), raising the possibility that these neurons might mediate the mCbN-dependent modulation of synaptic input to Chx10 neurons.
evidence: Supported by anatomical data shown in Figure 6A and citation to Suckow et al., 2013.

claim: The connectivity ratio for mCbN cells onto TH vlPAG neurons is 72.7%, with EPSCs of −35.2 ± 8.7 pA.
source: The connectivity ratio for mCbN cells onto TH vlPAG neurons was higher than onto Chx10 cells, with 72.7% of TH neurons (n = 8 of 11 cells [8 M, 0 F]) responding to optogenetic stimulation of mCbN afferents with EPSCs (Figure 6B,C, left; −35.2 ± 8.7 pA, n = 8), with a PPR of 0.8 ± 0.2 (Figure 6C, right; n = 8 cells).
evidence: Supported by electrophysiological recordings shown in Figure 6B and 6C.

claim: TH neurons in the vlPAG fire spontaneously at 17.9 ± 4.6 sp/s.
source: These TH neurons fired spontaneously (17.9 ± 4.6 sp/s, n = 8 cells [8 M, 0F]), as previously reported (Dougalis et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by electrophysiological recordings and citation to Dougalis et al., 2017.

claim: mCbN stimulation (30 light pulses at 25 Hz) accelerates spike onset in TH neurons, leading to a leftward shift of the cumulative interspike interval distribution.
source: The magnitude of the mCbN-dependent synaptic input evoked by 30 light pulses at 25 Hz was indeed sufficient to accelerate spike onset (Figure 6D), leading to a leftward shift of the cumulative interspike interval distribution (Figure 6E; control ISI: 112.7 ± 1.5 ms; +mCbN stimulated ISI: 100.0 ± 1.3 ms, n = 4 cells [4 M, 0 F]; p<0.0001, Kolmogorov-Smirnov test).
evidence: Supported by electrophysiological recordings shown in Figure 6D and 6E.

claim: mCbN stimulation increases TH neuron firing rate from 9.9 ± 0.1 spikes/sec to 11.2 ± 0.1 spikes/sec.
source: The leftward shift in the interspike interval distribution corresponded with a modest increase in firing rate (control: 9.9 ± 0.1 spikes/sec; +mCbN stimulation: 11.2 ± 0.1 spikes/sec, n = 4 cells [4M, 0F]).
evidence: Supported by electrophysiological recordings.

claim: Stimulating ChR2-expressing TH neurons increases eIPSCs in unlabeled vlPAG neurons from 139.5 ± 12.3 pA to 175.5 ± 17.3 pA, a within-cell increase of 27.0 ± 8.5%.
source: When the stimulus trains previously applied to mCbN cells were applied to TH-ChR2 cells, PSCs in unlabeled neurons were modulated similarly: eIPSCs increased in amplitude from 139.5 ± 12.3 pA to 175.5 ± 17.3 pA; (Figure 7A, n = 9 cells [2 M, 7 F]), giving a within-cell increase of 27.0 ± 8.5% (Figure 7B, left; p=0.013, one sample t-test) with no change in PPR (Figure 7B, right; 1.8 ± 0.06 vs. 2.0 ± 0.1, n = 9, p=0.84, paired t-test).
evidence: Supported by electrophysiological recordings shown in Figure 7A and 7B.

claim: Stimulating ChR2-expressing TH neurons decreases eEPSCs in unlabeled vlPAG neurons from −423.9 ± 85.9 pA to −340.9 ± 95.8 pA, a within-cell drop of 23.1 ± 7.7%.
source: Likewise, eEPSCs decreased from −423.9 ± 85.9 pA to −340.9 ± 95.8 pA (Figure 7C, n = 6 cells [4 M, 2 F]), corresponding to a within-cell drop of 23.1 ± 7.7% (Figure 7D, left; p=0.03, one sample t-test) with no change in PPR (Figure 7D, right; 0.8 ± 0.1 vs. 0.9 ± 0.1, p=0.4, paired t-test).
evidence: Supported by electrophysiological recordings shown in Figure 7C and 7D.

claim: Stimulation of TH-ChR2 neurons does not elicit direct EPSCs or IPSCs in unlabeled vlPAG cells.
source: Stimulation of TH-ChR2 neurons, however, did not elicit direct EPSCs (Figure 7E, top, F; peak pre-stimulus inward current: −3.5 ± 0.3 pA, peak post-stimulus inward current: −3.0 ± 0.4 pA p=0.3, n = 6 cells) or IPSCs (Figure 7E, bottom, F; peak pre-stimulus outward current: 4.4 ± 0.5 pA, peak post-stimulus outward current, 4.0 ± 0.6 pA, p=0.4, n = 9 cells) in unlabeled cells.
evidence: Supported by electrophysiological recordings shown in Figure 7E and 7F.

claim: Local co-release of glutamate or GABA from TH neurons in the vlPAG seems unlikely.
source: Local co-release of glutamate or GABA from TH neurons therefore seems unlikely.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that TH neuron stimulation does not elicit direct EPSCs or IPSCs.

claim: GDP-βS included in the pipette blocks the effects of TH cell stimulation on eIPSCs.
source: This manipulation blocked the effects of TH cell stimulation on eIPSCs, such that responses were 171.0 ± 26.5 pA before and 176.1 ± 26.0 pA after stimulation (Figure 7G, n = 6 cells [4 M, 2 F]). The within-cell change was thus reduced to 3.8 ± 2.8% (Figure 7H, left; p=0.24, one sample-t-test), with PPR remaining near 1 (Figure 7H, right; 1.1 ± 0.09 vs. 0.9 ± 0.1; p=0.07, paired t-test).
evidence: Supported by electrophysiological recordings shown in Figure 7G and 7H.

claim: GDP-βS prevents the modulation of IPSCs, providing evidence that the increase in IPSC amplitudes results from an altered postsynaptic response to GABA.
source: The observation that GDP-βS was sufficient to prevent the modulation of IPSCs provides further evidence that the increase in IPSC amplitudes results from an altered postsynaptic response to GABA, rather than from polysynaptic recruitment of additional inhibitory afferents to the recorded neurons.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that blocking postsynaptic G-protein signaling prevents IPSC modulation.

claim: Bath application of the D2 receptor agonist quinpirole (25 µM) increases IPSC amplitudes in Chx10 cells from 140.6 ± 13.8 pA to 217.8 ± 29.5 pA, a within-cell increase of 53.3 ± 10.4%.
source: Much like stimulation of TH-ChR2 cells, bath application of the D2 receptor agonist quinpirole (25 µM) increased IPSC amplitudes in Chx10 cells from 140.6 ± 13.8 pA to 217.8 ± 29.5 pA (Figure 8A; n = 5 cells [2 M, 3 F]), a within-cell increase of 53.3 ± 10.4% (Figure 8B; p=0.007, one sample t-test) and decreased eEPSCs from −262.1 ± 99.8 pA to −191.9 ± 87.7 pA (Figure 8C; n = 5 cells [1 M, 4 F]), a within-cell drop of 34.3 ± 11.3% (Figure 8D; p=0.04, one sample t-test).
evidence: Supported by electrophysiological recordings shown in Figure 8A and 8B.

claim: Bath application of the D2 receptor agonist quinpirole (25 µM) decreases eEPSCs in Chx10 cells from −262.1 ± 99.8 pA to −191.9 ± 87.7 pA, a within-cell drop of 34.3 ± 11.3%.
source: Much like stimulation of TH-ChR2 cells, bath application of the D2 receptor agonist quinpirole (25 µM) increased IPSC amplitudes in Chx10 cells from 140.6 ± 13.8 pA to 217.8 ± 29.5 pA (Figure 8A; n = 5 cells [2 M, 3 F]), a within-cell increase of 53.3 ± 10.4% (Figure 8B; p=0.007, one sample t-test) and decreased eEPSCs from −262.1 ± 99.8 pA to −191.9 ± 87.7 pA (Figure 8C; n = 5 cells [1 M, 4 F]), a within-cell drop of 34.3 ± 11.3% (Figure 8D; p=0.04, one sample t-test).
evidence: Supported by electrophysiological recordings shown in Figure 8C and 8D.

claim: Selectively activating D1 receptors does not significantly change PSC amplitudes in Chx10 neurons.
source: In contrast, selectively activating D1 receptors, by bath application of 10 µM dopamine with the D2 antagonist sulpiride (1 μM), did not significantly change PSC amplitudes. Activation of D1 receptors resulted in a within-cell change of 11.2 ± 17.7% in eIPSCs (Figure 8A,B, n = 5 cells [4 M, 1 F], p=0.8, one sample t-test) and a −0.9 ± 8.7% change in eEPSCs (Figure 8C,D; n = 5 cells [2 M, 3 F], p=0.6, one sample t-test).
evidence: Supported by electrophysiological recordings shown in Figure 8A, 8B, 8C, and 8D.

claim: The dopamine-dependent modulation of PSCs in Chx10 neurons is likely mediated by postsynaptic D2 receptors.
source: These data demonstrate that the dopamine-dependent modulation of PSCs in Chx10 neurons is likely mediated by postsynaptic D2 receptors.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that D2 agonist mimics the modulation while D1 activation does not.

claim: Bath application of sulpiride (1 μM) blocks the mCbN-induced modulation of eIPSCs in Chx10 neurons.
source: Bath application of sulpiride (1 μM), however, blocked both effects, such that in none of the 10 cells recorded in sulpiride did the extent of change reach the mean value for the modulated case. The eIPSCs of 246.8 ± 65.4 pA before stimulation remained at 246.4 ± 53.8 pA, a 3.1 ± 5.3% within-cell change (Figure 9A,B; n = 5 cells [5 M, 0 F], p=0.6, one sample t-test, % change vs. ACSF, p=0.03, unpaired t-test) and eEPSCs of −120.0 ± 14.7 pA before stimulation stayed at −122.1 ± 17.5 pA, a 1.0 ± 3.2% within-cell change (Figure 9C,D; n = 5 cells [3 M, 2 F], p=0.8, one sample t-test; % change vs. ACSF, p=0.005, unpaired t-test).
evidence: Supported by electrophysiological recordings shown in Figure 9A and 9B.

claim: Bath application of sulpiride (1 μM) blocks the mCbN-induced modulation of eEPSCs in Chx10 neurons.
source: Bath application of sulpiride (1 μM), however, blocked both effects, such that in none of the 10 cells recorded in sulpiride did the extent of change reach the mean value for the modulated case. The eIPSCs of 246.8 ± 65.4 pA before stimulation remained at 246.4 ± 53.8 pA, a 3.1 ± 5.3% within-cell change (Figure 9A,B; n = 5 cells [5 M, 0 F], p=0.6, one sample t-test, % change vs. ACSF, p=0.03, unpaired t-test) and eEPSCs of −120.0 ± 14.7 pA before stimulation stayed at −122.1 ± 17.5 pA, a 1.0 ± 3.2% within-cell change (Figure 9C,D; n = 5 cells [3 M, 2 F], p=0.8, one sample t-test; % change vs. ACSF, p=0.005, unpaired t-test).
evidence: Supported by electrophysiological recordings shown in Figure 9C and 9D.

claim: The mCbN-induced modulation of IPSC and EPSC strength onto Chx10 cells is mediated through activation of local dopaminergic interneurons within the vlPAG, via postsynaptically expressed D2 receptors.
source: Together, these results suggest that that the mCbN-induced modulation of IPSC and EPSC strength onto Chx10 cells is mediated through activation of local dopaminergic interneurons within the vlPAG, via postsynaptically expressed D2 receptors.
evidence: Inferred from the combined observations that TH neuron stimulation mimics mCbN effects, D2 agonist mimics the modulation, and D2 antagonist blocks mCbN-induced modulation.

claim: The cerebellum directly regulates midbrain regions that drive innate freezing in mice via glutamatergic projections from the mCbN.
source: Here, we demonstrate that the cerebellum directly regulates midbrain regions that drive innate freezing in mice, via glutamatergic projections from the mCbN that influence multiple classes of neurons in the vlPAG (schematized in Figure 10).
evidence: Summarizes the main findings of the study, supported by anatomical and electrophysiological data.

claim: Chx10 neurons are likely to generate freezing by directly exciting the Mc.
source: Since we find that Chx10 neurons are likely to generate freezing by directly exciting the Mc, the simplest interpretation is that mCbN activity stimulates dopamine release that biases the local circuit toward inhibition of Chx10 cells, thereby being permissive of movement.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that Chx10 neurons project to and excite Mc neurons, and optogenetic stimulation of Chx10 neurons elicits freezing.

claim: mCbN activity stimulates dopamine release that biases the local circuit toward inhibition of Chx10 cells, thereby being permissive of movement.
source: Since we find that Chx10 neurons are likely to generate freezing by directly exciting the Mc, the simplest interpretation is that mCbN activity stimulates dopamine release that biases the local circuit toward inhibition of Chx10 cells, thereby being permissive of movement.
evidence: Inferred from the combined observations that mCbN activates TH neurons, which modulate PSCs in Chx10 neurons to favor inhibition.

claim: Behavioral studies implicate activation of the cerebellar vermis, hence inhibition of the mCbN, as facilitating innate freezing.
source: Such a scenario would provide a mechanistic explanation for behavioral studies implicating activation of the cerebellar vermis, hence inhibition of the mCbN, as facilitating innate freezing.
evidence: Inferred from the present findings and previous behavioral studies showing that vermal lesions reduce freezing.

claim: The periaqueductal gray regulates a range of defensive behaviors, as activation of distinct rostro-caudal columns within the PAG elicits distinct responses such as flight (lPAG) or freezing (vlPAG).
source: The periaqueductal gray regulates a range of defensive behaviors, as activation of distinct rostro-caudal columns within the PAG elicits distinct responses such as flight (lPAG) or freezing (vlPAG) (Carrive, 1993; Bandler and Shipley, 1994; Behbehani, 1995; Bandler et al., 2000; Keay and Bandler, 2001).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies on PAG function.

claim: Optogenetic activation of glutamatergic vlPAG neurons that project to the Mc elicits freezing without analgesia in mice.
source: In vivo, optogenetic activation of glutamatergic vlPAG neurons that project to the Mc elicits freezing without analgesia in mice, whereas silencing of this cell population occludes innate freezing in response to threatening stimuli (Tovote et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Tovote et al., 2016.

claim: Silencing of glutamatergic vlPAG neurons that project to the Mc occludes innate freezing in response to threatening stimuli.
source: In vivo, optogenetic activation of glutamatergic vlPAG neurons that project to the Mc elicits freezing without analgesia in mice, whereas silencing of this cell population occludes innate freezing in response to threatening stimuli (Tovote et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Tovote et al., 2016.

claim: When threat probability is not all or none, firing rates in subsets of glutamatergic vlPAG neurons in rats correlate with the degree of danger, as do behavioral responses.
source: Additionally, when threat probability is not all or none, firing rates in subsets of glutamatergic vlPAG neurons in rats correlate with the degree of danger, as do behavioral responses (Wright and McDannald, 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to Wright and McDannald, 2019.

claim: The heterogeneous activity of glutamatergic vlPAG neurons suggests the existence of multiple classes of glutamatergic vlPAG cells.
source: The heterogeneous activity of glutamatergic vlPAG neurons, with distinct classes of response patterns evident, suggests the existence of multiple classes of glutamatergic vlPAG cells, which likely contribute differentially to assess threat probability and generate freezing (Wright and McDannald, 2019).
evidence: Inferred from the observation of heterogeneous activity patterns and citation to Wright and McDannald, 2019.

claim: The cerebellum has long been recognized as being involved in motor control.
source: The cerebellum has long been recognized as being involved in motor control, as disruptions of its signals give rise to disorders of movement, and experimentally elevating firing rates of CbN neurons can trigger muscle contraction (Noda and Fujikado, 1987; Hesslow, 1994a; Witter et al., 2013; Heiney et al., 2014; Proville et al., 2014; Lee et al., 2015).
evidence: Based on established scientific knowledge and citations to previous studies.

claim: Experimentally elevating firing rates of CbN neurons can trigger muscle contraction.
source: The cerebellum has long been recognized as being involved in motor control, as disruptions of its signals give rise to disorders of movement, and experimentally elevating firing rates of CbN neurons can trigger muscle contraction (Noda and Fujikado, 1987; Hesslow, 1994a; Witter et al., 2013; Heiney et al., 2014; Proville et al., 2014; Lee et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Cerebellar activity contributes to prediction on a sub-second timescale.
source: More generally, cerebellar activity contributes to prediction on a sub-second timescale (Ivry et al., 2002; Mauk and Buonomano, 2004; Molinari et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The cerebellum contributes to behaviors that carry a valence of reward or aversion.
source: It is also becoming clear that the cerebellum contributes to behaviors that carry a valence of reward or aversion (Kostadinov et al., 2019; Heffley and Hull, 2019; Carta et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to recent studies.

claim: The CbN projects directly to brainstem centers to alter, generate, or augment reflexes, such as those associated with the vestibulo-ocular reflex, eyelid conditioning, and whisking.
source: The CbN projects directly to brainstem centers to alter, generate, or augment reflexes, such as those associated with the vestibulo-ocular reflex, eyelid conditioning, and whisking (Lisberger, 1988; Medina et al., 2000; Brown and Raman, 2018); the cerebellum also forms multisynaptic loops with the cerebral cortex and hippocampus to modulate complex behaviors, including sensory discrimination and navigation (Popa et al., 2013; Proville et al., 2014; Rochefort et al., 2011; Babayan et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The cerebellum forms multisynaptic loops with the cerebral cortex and hippocampus to modulate complex behaviors, including sensory discrimination and navigation.
source: The CbN projects directly to brainstem centers to alter, generate, or augment reflexes, such as those associated with the vestibulo-ocular reflex, eyelid conditioning, and whisking (Lisberger, 1988; Medina et al., 2000; Brown and Raman, 2018); the cerebellum also forms multisynaptic loops with the cerebral cortex and hippocampus to modulate complex behaviors, including sensory discrimination and navigation (Popa et al., 2013; Proville et al., 2014; Rochefort et al., 2011; Babayan et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The cerebellar cortex receives and responds to signals from the vlPAG via both mossy fiber and climbing fiber inputs.
source: Previous studies have shown that the cerebellar cortex receives and responds to signals from the vlPAG via both mossy fiber and climbing fiber inputs (Watson et al., 2013; Koutsikou et al., 2014; Dietrichs, 1983; Apps and Strata, 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The vlPAG functionally connects to vermal regions of the cerebellum, and local cerebellar lesions of these areas disrupt learned fear responses.
source: The vlPAG functionally connects to vermal regions of the cerebellum, and local cerebellar lesions of these areas disrupt learned fear responses (Koutsikou et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Koutsikou et al., 2014.

claim: Synaptic plasticity in the cerebellar cortex is evident during fear conditioning training.
source: Moreover, synaptic plasticity in the cerebellar cortex is evident during fear conditioning training (Sacchetti et al., 2002; Sacchetti et al., 2004; Farley et al., 2016), consistent with the well-studied roles of Purkinje cells and their targets in motor learning (Medina et al., 2002).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Lesions of vermal Purkinje cells interfere with innate freezing.
source: Interestingly, however, lesions of vermal Purkinje cells (Supple et al., 1988; Koutsikou et al., 2014), which are expected to increase activity in the mCbN, also interfere with innate freezing, suggesting that cerebellar output facilitates movement.
evidence: Supported by citations to Supple et al., 1988 and Koutsikou et al., 2014.

claim: Directly suppressing cerebellar output from cerebellar nuclei can halt or slow movement even in non-associative complex or reflexive motor behaviors.
source: This observation is reminiscent of evidence that directly suppressing cerebellar output from other cerebellar nuclei can halt or slow movement even in non-associative complex or reflexive motor behaviors (Hesslow, 1994b; Goodkin and Thach, 2003; Sarnaik and Raman, 2018; Brown and Raman, 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: TH neurons in the PAG are implicated in several behaviors, including anti-nociception, sociability, fear learning, and arousal.
source: Interestingly, TH neurons in the PAG are implicated in several behaviors, including anti-nociception (Meyer et al., 2009; Li et al., 2016; Taylor et al., 2019), sociability (Matthews et al., 2016), fear learning (Groessl et al., 2018), and arousal (Porter-Stransky et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: TH neurons in the PAG may act either locally or via projections to regions such as the central amygdala and bed nucleus of the stria terminalis.
source: These TH neurons may act either locally or via projections to regions such as the central amygdala and bed nucleus of the stria terminalis (Li et al., 2013; Matthews et al., 2016; Li et al., 2016; Groessl et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.
